utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, you remain subject to the declaration which you made when you were here before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McLeod. We last met on May the 14th of this year. On that day, you testified that you had never heard of something called the HZ-HB. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that still true today; you still don't know what it is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I've done nothing to refresh my memory since we last met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know what the entity is, and you don't know what position, if any, Mr. Kordic held in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We touched briefly, on May the 14th, on your visit to the area of Ahmici and Vitez on May the 4th. Did you meet Colonel Stewart and converse with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was the commanding officer of the 1st Cheshire Regiment, I believe.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had personally seen 30 Croatian civilians or Croat civilians imprisoned in the silos in the village of Kacuni in conditions which were freezing cold and revolting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you discuss or have occasion to discuss with Colonel Stewart at all the kidnapping of Commander Zivko Totic on the evening of April 15th, 1993, in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing that with Colonel Stewart, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't recall any discussion by Colonel Stewart with the fact that that kidnapping seemed to him to be an incendiary spot which would caused the entire Lasva Valley to erupt in conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever express that view to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever express the view that the kidnapping of this senior Croat officer in a Muslim stronghold created a terribly volatile atmosphere in the valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart ever discuss with you the fact that he had personally seen about 1.000 Croats driven from their homes in the Lasva Valley region as a result of the fighting in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were a large number of Croats that had moved from Zenica to Vitez, and Colonel Stewart was concerned about that. I'm not sure that he actually discussed the matter precisely with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever express the view to you that he was of the opinion that Mr. Kordic was not a soldier at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you were of the view, and there was no question in your mind on this subject, that Colonel Blaskic was the HVO commander of Central Bosnia Operative Zone and that he was the military commander in the area on behalf of the HVO while you were present in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We discussed it last time, and you had little recollection on this. I would just like to ask you whether you've had any refreshed recollection on this subject. At page 20 of your notes, contemporaneous notes, you described a meeting with the Muslim military commander in Zenica, General Hadzihasanovic, Enver Hadzihasanovic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was of the view that it was best to go slowly. Do you remember putting that in your notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that he wanted to have the 7th Muslim Brigade under control rather than not; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you the Mujahedin were not under his control at that time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that, in fact, they were one of many elements that were not controlled in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of what those elements were, Mr. McLeod, the elements that weren't controlled?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We also touched briefly upon a meeting that you had with Colonel Ramiz Dugalic on May the 9th. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your notes, at page 55, and I don't know if you have them before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you'll have to remind me. There was a reference to notes. Now, I don't think we've got those, have we, or are they in the exhibits? We got the report which the witness made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to make the notes an exhibit, and I think we have copies for the Trial Chamber, although I wasn't anticipating using them all. I actually have some down in our locker, Your Honour, but I'm more than happy to make this an exhibit right now, and I'll distribute them as soon as we have a break, if I may, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D40/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got a copy of the notes in front of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have my original, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, the copy of your notes that has been provided to us have numbers up on the top right hand of the page. Does your copy have those numbers as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you would turn to page 55. Do I understand that this summarises at least part of your interview with Ramiz Dugalic on May the 9th?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dugalic gave you his view of who had been responsible for the Ahmici incidents, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Dugalic told you that the ABiH had actually captured two people at Ahmici, did he not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: He certainly said that they had, although as you're aware, I never actually got to see them, which is the point I think you're going to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's the point I was going to get to, but since you've covered it, I'll move on. I believe also that Colonel Blaskic, according to Mr. Dugalic, anyway, had given the order to do something. If you would just turn to the next page, I can't actually read your writing there. It's no criticism of you, sir, but I just can't make it out. It says, "Blaskic gave the order" to do something. Could you just inform the Trial Chamber what that says?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. Should I put it on the ELMO or should I simply read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea to put it on the ELMO for everybody.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: So as I indicate, Blaskic gave the order to put the man in the truck, and Darko Kraljevic carried out the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what you meant by "Blaskic gave the order to put the man or men in the truck"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's referring, I think, to an attack on Stari Vitez that was carried out by driving a truck into the town. There was certainly an incident which had taken place with a truck bomb, and that's what he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just so that we have it in mind, all this appears in the report. Annex "I" has the interview with the particular gentleman. Perhaps I could ask the Prosecution, is there anything more in the notes than is in the report? Can you recollect that, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my general recollection would be they are certainly not verbatim, exact, but I have reviewed them. I can't say I've reviewed every single word myself, but the pages I have reviewed tend to follow closely the typed version, and I think Mr. McLeod has testified, both in this court and previously, that essentially, when he typed up the annexes to his report, he essentially sat at a computer or word processor with his notes and typed them. So I would say, Your Honour, in most respects, as known to me, they are extremely similar, but I would hesitate to say that they are exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to pick up the pace a little bit, if I may, Mr. McLeod, so that we can get your cross-examination completed as soon as possible. You have been, I believe, the prosecuting officer at about a dozen courts martial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These judicial proceedings have been conducted exclusively by military judicial authorities, have they not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In all of the proceedings that you've been involved in, there has not been any involvement by politicians in the process, has there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've not ever heard of a situation where politicians have been obliged somehow to monitor the progress of military investigations or prosecutions, have you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: We could either have a complicated answer or a very simple "no," so we'll keep it simple, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: In all of the prosecutions that you've participated in, no politician has had any kind of duty to make sure that the progression goes forward; that's a matter purely for the wheels of military justice, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: To take a slightly more complicated answer, in that case, in the United Kingdom, military law is passed by statute, and that's passed by politicians. So if you like, actually the whole thing is set up by the politicians in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, I see, but the actual administration of military justice itself is a matter that proceeds independently of political involvement, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you referred to the Vance-Owen Plan in response to a question by Judge Bennouna, and to the intent to hold elections after what you refer to as population shifts. Do you know when the first democratic elections were held in either the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as to these population shifts, insofar as they involved some Croats in the Zenica area, you referred, I believe, to the term "self-cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that I was asked the question, had I actually heard of the term "self-cleansing" being used, and I think my answer was no, in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Then I don't need to spend any more time on that. We've gone over, in rather laborious detail, already, the mass burnings, killings, and plundering of Croat villages in the Zenica area in your previous cross-examination and in your report appendices. Are you familiar with a document that was drafted by the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights, the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, dated the 17th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I know that you're not familiar with the document, but the factual contention is made in this document that the forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, conservatively, killed about 120 Croat civilians between April and September of 1993. Do you have any reason to disagree with that figure?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You testified previously that the HVO commander in chief in Bosnia-Herzegovina was General Milivoj Petkovic. Does that name sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever try to speak with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, just a few questions on the distinction between the HVO and the HDZ. I believe that you previously testified that the Croat authorities had established a military organisation called the HVO and a political organisation called the HDZ. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If I may, I'd just like to show you one exhibit, which is annex II to the trial brief that has been filed by the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an exhibit, by any standards. What point do you want to make, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just that there are a large quantity of people both -- at the national level whose offices are identified in the HDZ and in the HVO, Your Honour, and on the local level, as well, the party political organisation and the military organisation, and that Mr. Kordic is only identified as having a role within the HZ-HB and as a member of the HDZ BiH. He was not involved at the local, political, or military level in Busovaca, and he was not involved at the national military level in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you've made that point. You don't need to make it again. I don't think it's a suitable one for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few final questions, sir. If you had been given more time, more than the one-week time limit that was imposed upon you by your superiors at the ECMM, you would have been able to interview all of these political figures in Busovaca and Zenica, and the military figures, too, that you were not able to fit into your hectic schedule during the week that you were in the Lasva Valley; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you had more than just four and a half days to do all of your interviews, you would have to concede that this would have given you a fuller and more complete understanding of the political and the military situation in the area, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as consequence, your report would have been more complete and thoughtful without that one-week deadline, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you did your best to make sure that you used the time available to you to maximum effect, given the tasks that were imposed upon you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You made sure that to the maximum extent possible, you interviewed all of the most important people in the region?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Spoke to them about the political and the military situation and any other items that fell within your charge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you made sure that you discussed with these people all of the important events in the past few months in the Lasva Valley; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You stressed to them that you needed and were seeking all pertinent information relating to those events that you could possibly gather and assemble; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two final questions for you, sir, if I may. The first one is this. Of the three policemen that you interviewed in Busovaca, and the interview that you had with Colonel Blaskic, the interview that you had with Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak in Vitez, and the two Catholic priests in Zenica and Cajdras, Father Stjepan and Father Bozo, it's true, isn't it, that the name "Mr. Kordic" didn't arise once?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name may have been mentioned, but it's quite correct that it is not actually written down in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have no recollection of his name being mentioned, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final question, sir: On the Muslim side, you interviewed the mayor of Zenica, Besim Spahic; you interviewed the military commander of the 3rd Corps headquartered in Zenica, general Hadzihasanovic; you met his chief of staff, Ramiz Dugalic, a colonel; you met representatives of the International Committee for the Red Cross. And isn't it true that the name "Mr. Kordic" was not mentioned by any of those people, either, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, it's true that it's not written down in my notes as being something which came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's true that as far as you can remember, none of those people that I've just recited mentioned the name "Mr. Kordic" at any time during your interviews of them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question to answer, as I'm sure you're aware. The precise answer is no, I can't remember. We'll leave it at that, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McLeod. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this case I represent, together with my colleague, Kovacic, the second accused, Mr. Cerkez. Allow me to put several questions to you, and please answer them to best of your recollection, if you will. Mr. McLeod, you have explained your tasks, the assignment you had in Central Bosnia. My question is the following: At that time, were you familiar with any of the languages spoken in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was getting some understanding, some comprehension of Serbo-Croat, but I would certainly not claim to be a fluent speaker of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the talks and interviews that you had from the 7th to the 11th of May, 1993, were conducted in English with the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was speaking in English, and the people I was talking to were speaking in their language through an interpreter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, Mr. McLeod, how the interpreters were recruited for these interviews that you had? Did you bring interpreters from your mission in Zagreb, or was the interpreter provided in Zenica, or from some other place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The interpreters that I was using were provided by the ECMM in Zenica, and I think with the exception of my meeting with Colonel Blaskic, where, as I've indicated, his interpreter actually took over the translating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you right, that that was the only case -- that is, when you spoke to Colonel Blaskic -- that you had an interpreter brought by the side that was being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, can you remember what ethnic group the interpreters that were put at your disposal in Zenica belonged to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that one of the interpreters that I was using was Muslim. I don't know who Jean-Pierre Thebault's interpreter was at all, and I assume that Colonel Blaskic was using a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So am I right in saying that in all the talks except in the talks with Colonel Blaskic, an interpreter of Muslim ethnicity was used?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: One could assume that, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, at the time, you must have been aware of the tensions in inter-ethnic relations between the Croats and the Muslims, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In spite of that, you didn't think that perhaps it would be better to use an interpreter belonging to another ethnic group for your talks, except for always using members of the same ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it would be reasonable to say that throughout my experience of years of working in the former Yugoslavia, I used interpreters who came from a very wide range of backgrounds, including some who were not even nationals of the former Yugoslavia, and without exception they were extremely good at doing their jobs and keeping their personal thoughts to themselves. So in practice, although what you're suggesting would be a good theory, it didn't happen and was not really a problem, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you for this specific case for the period of fighting between the Croatian and Muslim entities in Bosnia, where you happened to be at that precise time.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think under the circumstances, what we were doing was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honour, perhaps I could move this faster. If Mr. Mikulicic has some reason to believe that something was wrongly translated, maybe he could go specifically to that passage. If not, I think we're talking in theoretical generalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a direct question, as suggested by my learned friend. Mr. McLeod, are you absolutely certain that the interpreter you used quite correctly, absolutely correctly, interpreted the statements given to you? Is your knowledge of the local language sufficient for you to be able to check the interpretations you were given?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that they were doing their best to be as accurate as they could be, which under the circumstances was the best that we could have, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think we've exhausted this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Let us move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, how did you note down the statements of the persons you interviewed? Did you use a recording machine?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that I've testified previously I sat and wrote in my notebook as the interviews were going on, and to a large extent, as there was an interpreter being used, there would be a pause between somebody saying something and then me getting a chance to write it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you able to discern from your notes what the person being interviewed told you from what you put down as your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think in some cases, it's quite clear because of the terminology that's being used. In other cases, and again we've discussed this at some length, there are some bits where I'm not sure whether what I'm writing is my comment or is something that was actually being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, before arriving in Central Bosnia, did you familiarise yourself with the culture and history of the parts of the land that you were going to visit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, to a limited extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you also study the political circumstances that preceded the events of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that I was observing them by being part of the mission that was actually watching what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. McLeod, did you have any idea as to the reasons of the conflict in Central Bosnia between the Croatian and Muslim entities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I had as clear an idea as anybody else that was there from the International Community that was watching.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The two or, indeed, the three different ethnic groups had been living in Central Bosnia together for quite some time and had been maintaining an easy or uneasy relationship with each other for quite some time. And over a period of years, as the Cold War came to an end, this situation had started to deteriorate and various elements of nationalism were trying to exert themselves, and one could see how the situation had deteriorated into the events that I was then involved in watching and attempting to try and relieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod -- I beg your pardon. The transcript is correct after all. Mr. McLeod, are you aware of the fact that from the beginning of the conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and, of course, also in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the International Community had tried to mitigate or, rather, deal with the problem? To be more specific, were you aware of the meeting in the Villa Konak held on the 17th and 18th of March, 1992, chaired by Mr. Cutilliero and with the participation of Messrs. Boban, Izetbegovic and Karadzic, when a solution was offered for the political setup in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of the results of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that occasion, the three representatives of the entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the Serbs, Croats and Muslims, had agreed on the ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't doubt that that was what was going on, but at this stage six years later, I can't remember the precise details, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, may I remind you, with the help of a map, and then perhaps that will refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So with the assistance of the usher, please, could we distribute this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if we are going on to discuss the meeting, the witness has said that he wasn't aware of the results, so there's little point putting anything to him. No doubt, if you want to call evidence about this, Mr. Mikulicic, of course you'll be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Mr. President. I was going to tender this as evidence, but perhaps I should try a different route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness, Mr. McLeod, are you familiar with the basis of the so-called Vance-Owen Plan on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into cantons based on the ethnic principle?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, in that case, let me show you a map showing Bosnia-Herzegovina and the division into cantons as envisaged by the Vance-Owen Plan, and then I will have only two brief questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These exhibits are marked D41/1 and D42/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I point out that these are Defence exhibits that have been recorded under the number "/2". Perhaps that is how they should be numbered, "/2".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll just get the numbers put right. They should be "/2". Are they the right numbers, 41 and 42?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, we'll get the numbers later, perhaps, so as not to waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, please look at this Vance-Owen map marked with the numbers "8" and "10", the cantons which, according to that plan, should have been under the control of the Croatian entity. Tell me, according to your knowledge of the conditions there, do these cantons include the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me, but the copy of the map I've got is so unclear that it's not actually easy for me to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that, Mr. McLeod. I'm not asking you to read the map, just to tell us, on the basis of your own knowledge, whether these are the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and Travnik that should have, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, been part of canton number 10. If you don't know, don't trouble yourself any further.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry, but I think that not only can I not identify which of the cantons on the map, but I'm not sure whether this is one of the iterations of the Vance-Owen Plan which ended up having any significance or not. So I think that I would rather not answer or attempt to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on then, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Mikulicic. As you're referring to the Vance-Owen Plan again, I should like to ask Mr. McLeod about what is called "control" in the Vance-Owen Plan. What does it actually mean, control by such and such an ethnic group, when talking about the Vance-Owen Plan? Then it says, "Under Bosniak, under Croat, under Serb control." You're familiar with the contents of that plan, so you know what is meant when the word "control" is used?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, the idea was to establish political and military and judicial police structures, the membership of which or the hierarchy of which would be based on the underlying ethnic structure that was in place in whichever of the cantons that one was referring to. So I believe one would expect to see, in a majority Croat area, that the majority of the military, police and political leadership would be Croats as opposed to Serbs or Muslims and so on. Things became particularly difficult in areas where the ethnic mix was fairly evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Therefore, what is referred to as "control" simply means a majority chosen by such an ethnic group, based on the population composition in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For clarification's sake, these two maps were admitted in the Aleksovski case through the testimony of Professor Bianchini and on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be, but we're dealing with this case, and I notice that the second of the maps isn't the Vance-Owen Plan at all, but it's the division agreed by the parties in the Villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My question, Mr. President, for the witness is whether, between these two maps, in view of the areas marked as belonging to one or the other entity, whether he sees any noticeable difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not a matter for him. That's a matter for argument for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, in your examination in chief, you said that you had the impression that the events of the 16th of April were carefully planned and coordinated, and in support of that thesis, you said that on the very morning of the 16th of April, there were massive arrests and detentions of more prominent persons of Muslim ethnicity in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) in your report, Mr. McLeod, in this context, you also added a list to be found in appendix 2 of annex A. That is a list of 13 leading Muslims arrested in Vitez. Would you be kind enough to look at that list? For Their Honours, this is appendix 2 to annex A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, will you please tell us who gave you the information that these 13 persons were arrested on the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, this information that you used as an argument in your statement, did you check it in any way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I met one of the men who had been arrested and had a brief conversation with him in his home, and I met a number of the other men who had been arrested in Kaonik prison, and the fact of the matter did not appear to be disputed by the Croats. I think again we can find the reference in one of the conversations that I had about the fact that people had been arrested and most of them had now been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. According to this list, Mr. McLeod, the first person on the list is Munib Kajmovic, the president of the SDA of Vitez. Mr. Munib Kajmovic testified in this Tribunal less than a month ago, and he himself told me that he had never been arrested. What would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness can't comment on that. It's what another witness has told the Tribunal, if that's right. That's a matter for you to comment on when you come to make submissions to us. It's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, in your report you have attached another list, a list of captured persons held in the Kaonik prison. Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it is, please, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, in my copy, the copy is a poor one, so I can't see the number. But it says "02047". This is the list I'm talking about. Maybe it would be helpful if I showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got it, Mr. McLeod? Do you have the list that's being referred to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's on the ELMO at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my report, it's "01-1", but then it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, would you be so kind as to tell us where you got this list from? Who gave it to you, or did you compile it yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I've testified previously in the court, it was given to me by Mr. Aleksovski, whom I understood was the man who was running the prison in Kaonik, and he gave it to me when I was visiting the prison. The list was printed off the computer system which he controlled, and I believe that it was a list of the people that, according to his computer system, if nothing else, were currently resident in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We see on this list, Mr. McLeod, something added by hand and other comments on a typewriter. Could you explain to us who the author is of those additions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. So at the top, this is typed by myself and is simply the reference which allows the list to be incorporated into my report. Then here again we have my rather familiar and indecipherable handwriting (indicating), and that was written while I was actually in the prison itself. Then right at the very bottom, again my handwriting, just incorporating the page number so that the pages could be found within the report. I believe that's everything that's been added to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the next page of this report. These remarks that you say you wrote yourself by hand, what do they actually represent? Is it information that you received or, rather, your comments?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that what I was doing, and again at this distance in time I can't remember precisely, but what I think I was doing was as I went into the cell in which these men were contained, I was making a note of the previous occupation, if you like, of what the person had been doing before, and then the day when they had been arrested. So you can see "16/04", "16/4", so that really would be the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the date of their arrest. Did you verify that date in the documents or is it the date you took down on the basis of your conversation with those persons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that while we were having these brief conversations in the cell, they were saying -- I was identifying who the people were after a while, and they were saying, "This is who I am. I was a forensic in Vitez police, and I was arrested on the 16th of April." I would certainly not have written myself "forensic in Vitez police," which is what I think it was -- as it was being translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are talking of the person under number 74 in this list, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But that same person, in his statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, said that he was arrested on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's another point, not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. We won't dwell on that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, when we're talking about Kaonik, did you manage to learn under whose jurisdiction that facility, that prison in Kaonik, was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Having had several conversations with people about it, the policemen that I met in Busovaca and Mr. Aleksovski, I believe that it was a military prison under military jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have in front of me your notes that you made after talking to the head of the civilian police in Busovaca, Mr. Nikica Petrovic, where it says that the prison was under the jurisdiction of the military court in Travnik. Is this something that you learned? Is it your conclusion? Or is it what he told you? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you check that fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: In no more detail than having Mr. Aleksovski also explain that it was a military prison. I can't remember whether Aleksovski actually said that it was under the military court in Travnik or not. But we could go and check it, even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, do you know that prior to the 16th of April -- that is, on the 15th of April, 1993 -- in the municipality building in Vitez, a meeting was held of a commission for incidents which was composed of representatives of two ethnic groups, of the Muslim entity and the Croatian entity, and that that commission adopted certain conclusions? Are you familiar with that fact and the conclusions of that commission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm aware that a joint commission was meeting. I'm not specifically aware of that meeting or of the conclusions of that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. McLeod. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the map relating to the Vance-Owen Plan will be D30/1, and the number for the other map will be D31/2 -- sorry; D30/2 and D31/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, by the time you arrived in Central Bosnia in May of 1993, you had previously been a trained, if you will, military observer both in Northern Ireland, for approximately two years, and also previously during your ECMM involvement in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And based on that experience, you had some past training and qualification in terms of observing what was happening in a local environment; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers has asked you a long series of questions about various other events or alleged atrocities in Central Bosnia, many of them allegedly involving Croat victims. Mr. McLeod, can you tell the Court, was it ever your intention, in the middle of May 1993, to catalogue and discuss every such event or alleged event in Central Bosnia during the first six months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it in fact likely that there were also a number of other events or atrocities involving alleged Muslim victims which you also did not include in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On a particular topic, if I can ask the usher to hand you what's marked as Defence exhibit 25/1, I wonder if I can direct your attention to the heading -- well, first of all, for the record, is this a special report on Croats in Zenica dated the 20th -- well, concerning the period or the date of the report, 20 and 21 of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It might be helpful, for the courtroom's reference, to put that on the ELMO, Mr. Usher. If you could just move it down momentarily so the counsel and Court can see just the title and format of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is an ECMM-prepared document around the same time, roughly, the end of April, early May, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Evidencing, would you agree, some concern and interest by ECMM in what was happening to the Croats in the area, as well as the Muslims? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention specifically to item number 1, titled "Zenica's Prison." Directing your attention to approximately the third line, the end of the third line, the report states: "They are well treated, considering the situation."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Given what you had in front of you, in terms of your report and the material you were trying to cover in the time that you were in Central Bosnia, was it perhaps the case that there was less concern for the Croat prisoners in this particular situation than what you were hearing about the Muslim prisoners at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think, actually, it would be fair to say that there was equal concern for prisoners on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fair enough. And were you able to determine and had ECMM been able to determine during this time period that at least concerning Zenica prison, the Croat prisoners there were, all things, in a terrible situation, admittedly, but in that situation, they were being treated well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly what this report is saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you testified some weeks ago now, in direct, that you arrived in Central Bosnia on this assignment with an open mind, with no preconceived conclusions; is that still your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Despite all the cross-examination that you've now had from both counsel, you still believe that you entered this mission with an open mind?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was my -- that was my best intention, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise for interrupting you. Can you explain to the Court when and how, in the course of your mission and the preparation of your report, did your thinking begin to be formed in any particular direction? When did you begin to arrive at particulars sets of conclusions which then, ultimately, of course, became your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think at the point where I was sitting down and reading the various sitreps, ECMM and UNPROFOR, that we've discussed previously, and plotting out where events had happened and seeing that there were a number of events which had happened at almost exactly the same time, suggesting not just an isolated incident, as the first issue. Then the second stage was reaching the conclusion that in a number, if not the majority, of cases, events had been instigated by the Croatian side rather than the Muslim side, and therefore what one appeared to have was a coordinated effort, in a number of places at the same time, as opposed to one isolated incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were sent on this mission from your base in the humanitarian section in the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you were essentially to be part of what was essentially a three-person team along with Ambassador Thebault and Mr. Friis-Pedersen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were Ambassador Thebault and Mr. Friis-Pedersen what you might, in this particular setting, call more locals than you were, in terms of this was their local, on-the-ground assignment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And had been for some time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you prepared your report and circulated a draft of your report, did either Ambassador Thebault or Mr. Friis-Pedersen disagree with you, suggest that you didn't know what you were talking about, suggest that you had not accurately observed what was happening in Central Bosnia during that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by the time that your report was prepared and submitted to your management, did Ambassador Thebault and Mr. Friis-Pedersen agree in and join your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault certainly did. I'm not sure that Erik had commented in detail on the final summary, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask -- I'm sorry; go ahead. Let me ask a follow-up, similar question, then. During the course of your work with Mr. Friis-Pedersen on this project, did he ever indicate disagreement with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour; I'm sorry. Your Honours, in this regard, I make a point for the record that before Mr. McLeod leaves the Tribunal, I would ask that the Defence -- I would offer that the Defence put any question to Mr. McLeod concerning any disagreements or any conflict they might purport to find between his testimony in the report and a transcript of Mr. Friis-Pedersen's testimony, and I say so for this reason: because Mr. Friis-Pedersen is one of the witnesses who died. The Court has accepted the transcript. The Defence also has his full statement, and in light of the attacks on Mr. McLeod's qualifications and methodology, if they can find something in either his testimony or his statement that contradicts his report or his testimony, I think the witness should have a chance to confront that before he leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there is anything, it will be matter for comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, on cross-examination, suggested that you had not met with any of the Croat military leaders, but in fact you did meet with Mr. Blaskic; true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your direct examination and in cross, you mentioned that there were three schools of thought circulating, if you will, at the time about what had happened in Ahmici. I'm happy to ask you to state those yourself, but if there is no objection, in the interest of time, I'll try to summarise it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard it, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court recalls it, just because it was some weeks ago, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You recall this basic testimony, very, very shorthand, either the Muslims attacked the village, their own people; there had been something called agents provocateurs, or the Serbs had attacked the village, the areas, to destabilise or create conflict between the Muslims and the Croats; or that, indeed, the HVO had mounted a deliberate attack on the Muslim population. Those were essentially the three schools of thought?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Among other things, on page 1 of your report, you concluded it was hard to believe that each of the acts were the result of isolated extremist -- or groups; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, you're not re-examining; you're merely going over the old evidence. Well, I'm about to -- yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're coming to a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my final set of questions will relate to questions which -- I have a packet to give the Court. It's only for the purposes of reference by the Court, not for the witness, but unless there's -- it has to do with prior testimony, and unless there's -- the Court, and I think counsel, can follow and make sure that they think that it's an accurate representation by me, I simply think it will be easier if I hand out this information, which, again, will be the basis of about ten questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say "prior testimony"; which testimony is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is the testimony of the defendant Blaskic in his trial, Your Honour, in contrast to what was told to this witness when Mr. McLeod interviewed him on May 8th of 1993, as opposed to the statements and conclusions of Mr. Blaskic in terms of the attack on Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How does this arise from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is extensive questioning of this witness's credibility and the manner in which he prepared his report and that there was not an adequate basis for him to reach these conclusions. The proof is in the pudding, I submit, Your Honour, and the proof, as would come out and is supported by a senior Bosnian Croat military leader, is that, in his own testimony, his own case, under oath, is that Mr. McLeod's assessment was exactly spot on the money, contrary to the Defence attacks that it is incredible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think you can support your own witness in that way, not by asking him about what Mr. Blaskic said. If you've got some other means of getting that before the Trial Chamber, you could certainly do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask, then, a very similar, abbreviated set of questions, then, Your Honour? I won't take the time to pass these out, but I think I can make the point in a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One of the -- well, we all know by now one of the individuals you interviewed was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for a point of reference, Your Honour, that is at G1, appendix G1 to Mr. McLeod's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At any time in the course of your interview with General Blaskic on the 8th of May, 1993, just a few weeks after the attack on Ahmici, did he indicate to you his conclusion that the attack on Ahmici was a crime?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you at any time that in fact it was an organised, systematic, and planned crime under somebody's control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the thesis that he was putting forward was that everything that had happened had been as a reaction to a Muslim attack, and so the organisation was on his part, but as a reaction under counter-attack. That was quite clear in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you at that time that he had or contemplated asking an investigation be conducted by an SIS officer by the name of Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following your mission in Central Bosnia, were you ever provided a copy of a report by Anto Sliskovic submitted to Mr. Blaskic on the 25th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the course of your discussion with Colonel Blaskic these few days after the attack on Ahmici, did he indicate to you that it was his view that the HVO military police had committed the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he tell you at that time that he had told this to General Petkovic, the chief of staff of the HVO? That he had told General Petkovic that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. There's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I would object on that line of questioning. As you rightly said a day or so ago, it is not Blaskic here on trial. I don't see the relevance, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I rather agree. If you want to make a point Mr. Scott, you must do it later in the trial; but doing it through this witness, in this way, when we have the report in front of us, does not assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, if I can ask one closing question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Colonel Blaskic had in fact given you such information when you interviewed him on the 8th of May, 1993, would that have been consistent with and in fact supported your conclusions in terms of what happened, how the attack on Ahmici was carried out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: If he had had evidence that the attack had been carried out by the Croatian side, then that would have been consistent with the conclusion that I reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to make the point that very often, it seems to me that cross-examination and re-examination are conducted in this trial as though there are no further stages in the trial, when in fact there is open to both sides the process of making submissions at the end of the Prosecution's case as well as the address at the end of the case. And it seems to me that there is a limit to what you can extract from a witness. I have noticed quite frequently that counsel makes a good point in cross-examination and yet wants to extract more from the witness, when that should really be an appropriate matter for submission at the end of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, thank you for coming, and also coming back to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to go, if you would like to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, if that's what you had in mind, can I just explain what the present position is as to evidence? There's no more evidence, I think, this week. Possibly there will be a short witness tomorrow. The reason for that is that last Friday's witness spilled over into this week. The witness listed for Monday could only come on Monday, and I think Tuesday, so he was stood down. It wasn't then known how long the evidence would take. It was known that there was to be discussion about the dossier, and in those circumstances, no further witness has been sought, and it's not at all sure that even if I had sought one, I would have been able to find one at short notice simply to fill what would have been, at best, part of half a day. I'm sorry about that. There remains the witness Ehsan Bajwa, who took the statement from Dr. Mujezinovic, who can I think can be called conveniently tomorrow, but he won't take very long. We have been in discussion with Ms. Featherstone throughout the week, both sides, as to time tabling, and I think the Defence have come here today expecting the dossier issue to be argued tomorrow. I see that they are nodding on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there's Mr. Alcock's or Dr. Alcock's evidence to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That we have also resolved amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you what the position is there. I've discussed it with Mr. Stein. So far as he is concerned, his report, in English, was received by us on the 25th of June and filed 15 minutes after receipt, sent down for translation, and under all pressure, the translation didn't return until the 10th of July. There may be an issue at some stage to be determined, in respect of experts, what is the requirement for a translation into a language the defendant understands, because it's not explicitly covered by any earlier order. Setting that technical issue on one side, Mr. Stein and I have agreed the position about next week's evidence as follows. The first witness, Donia, who comes in on Monday for a week when we have four afternoons of evidence, is a witness I shall take very shortly in chief; I'm not quite sure how short, but very short, or short. Notwithstanding that, Mr. Stein is sure that his examination will last at least until Wednesday, as I understand it, which will leave only, at most, if he's right, half a day and a bit for Alcock. Alcock I will again take shortly in chief, or whoever takes him will take him shortly in chief, and again, Mr. Stein is confident that his cross-examination will exhaust the week and will involve Alcock coming back at some future date. In those circumstances, he accepts that any inconvenience or difficulty that they may face arising from the fact that they didn't have the translated version for their clients any earlier than the 21st of July, whatever their entitlement under the Rules, can be cured by dealing with issues arising on an adjourned date. Now, that's, I hope you will agree, a sensible resolution of any problem. It is of course contingent on Mr. Stein's estimates of time to be taken being accurate, but I hope I have faithfully reflected what he has told me. He nods assent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The only addition being, visualising the calendar in my head, the next week, the week after next, is consumed with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So we presume Alcock would therefore come on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some other date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- some other date. That would cure the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to both experts, one of whose reports is compact, the other of whose is long, I will be serving on everybody, I hope, if not today, tomorrow, an overview -- in one case I think it's about three sides; in the other it's probably only one -- which will guide you to the conclusions and the central pages, and I hope that will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. So is the position this, that -- one short witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we really must try and deal with the dossier argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. As to that, although I think the detail to be argued tomorrow, and Mr. Smith, who I think wishes -- oh, he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's adjourn now and take our break. We will resume this after the break. We're not sitting beyond 5.15 today. A quarter of an hour now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we move on to the dossier, Judge Bennouna has a point arising from the matters which were mentioned just before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My question has been prompted by what we learned from the discussion between the Prosecution and the Defence, Mr. Nice and Mr. Stein, regarding the subject of Mr. Donia. Your estimate, and I hope it is overestimated because we do not at all intend to listen to Mr. Donia until the end of Wednesday, can you reassure us, because in our view we should finish with Donia by Tuesday to hear another witness on Wednesday. You see that the rhythm that we are applying now is intended to make good progress and within reasonable time limits. So can you reassure me on this point, and then I can go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I cannot reassure you. I wish I could. Mr. Donia, Dr. Donia, is an expert witness. He covers much territory. I do not intend to discuss medieval times with him. You won't be hearing that. He has testified in Blaskic. He covers broadly and widely, he paints with a broad brush, and I'm quite sure that I will go into Wednesday with him to give you the full account of what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, subject to what we say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Subject to the Court, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure you won't waste any time, and I hope it's going to be possible to deal with the matter more rapidly, particularly if the examination in chief is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We had proposed, and I thought this was given, that there would be limited if no examination in chief. You would have had the report and read it. That is the way we were going to operate, and that's fine with us. So it was presume I would pretty much jump in, if the Court would allow, on Monday and start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Therefore, if you begin straightaway on Monday, we can hope that you will have finished by Tuesday afternoon, if the examination in chief is very short. But you will do your best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I will be working on it this weekend and paring it down, but my best estimate right now, I can tell you, with the Court's permission, would be Wednesday, but I will work towards Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Now, we turn to the dossier which we've had, in fact I have here beside me, our copy of it. The position now is that we've had the investigator's report, we have had the response from both accused to the dossier, and perhaps the most orderly way of dealing with it would be to invite the Prosecution to begin, in the light of the latest pleadings, as it were, and then we'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the latest pleadings leave the position in a sense substantially unchanged from what I forecast they would be. The Defence, in slightly different ways in their two pleadings, have effectively admitted nothing. Their grounds for challenging are, I think in general, three; one, there's a matter in issue, the nature of the attack and defence of the village; two, there's a witness who is unwilling to attend, that being in itself a ground to say that his evidence should not be read; three, and this is most to be found at the last part of the response on behalf of Kordic, matters are outside the knowledge, it is said, of Kordic and therefore there's no way in which those matters can be admitted. There are maps and so on that are admitted, but they don't take us very much further. Even prior testimony, although it was once said by Mr. Smith, I can remember, that prior testimony might be admissible, is challenged, and we really get nowhere on the basis of the pleadings of the defendants. The reality is that the single issue highlighted is whether evidence has to be live from the witness box or whether it can come in the form of, as argued here, written statements. That issue, I forecast, will lie at the root both of this problem and, indeed, of some other problems yet to face this Chamber. First, there is the outstanding issue of a dead witness whose statement we seek to have read. You will recall that on an earlier occasion, we dealt with two dead witnesses and the prior testimony of one of them, but left outstanding the issue of the statement of the dead witness. There is another issue, I think, which will be coming, probably, to be dealt with at some stage, and that is what, if anything, should be done in respect of witnesses who are unwilling, perhaps through fear, from coming to the Tribunal at all. Of course, it's a little early for me to be sure that a witness is definitely unwilling to come and that it's through fear, because there's some time to pass before the end of my case, and therefore further efforts can be made to secure the attendance of witnesses and, indeed, to check on their attitude. But if witnesses are unwilling to attend and if it is through reasonable fear, there will be an argument advanced the Tribunal should consider their written statements as evidence in the case, on the basis not least of common sense that if a witness had something material to offer an inquiry of this kind and is not available in the conventional way through reasons entirely genuine of that kind, how can it be proper that the Tribunal should not have the advantage of considering what he or she was able to say. But that's for a later date. There may be other ways of dealing with those particular issues. The argument may not arise in exactly that way, but I simply forecast that the issue of the reading of witness statements is not entirely particular to this application. We've set out earlier in our skeleton argument why we say that written statements may indeed be admitted. They are a species of evidence. They are identical in concept to hearsay evidence that the Tribunal does accept through witnesses from time to time. There is therefore no straightforward or unanswerable reason why the statements should not be read, and it will be a matter, as the Court knows from our argument, will be a matter for the Chamber to decide whether a particular statement should be read or, indeed, whether that witness should be called. I can tell you that so far as the witnesses in the dossier are concerned, originally we had identified four as being, I think in our earlier categorisation of witnesses, above the line, and that's numbers 10, 11, and 13, and one who has already given evidence, he being above the line. We had forecast being able to deal with matters such as the autopsy, a document which is now challenged in full by the Defence for various reasons. We had forecast being able to deal with that without perhaps a witness being called, and none had been served formally to produce it. Were the Defence argument saying that even that document is inadmissible is to be upheld, then we would have to consider adding to the list. Indeed, the attitude of the Defence shows how, in a sense, insincere, and I don't mean that offensively, but how insincere was their suggestion to the Tribunal at an earlier stage that the Prosecution should be limited essentially to two witnesses per village. As I said in the skeleton argument we advanced, had anybody fallen for that, all that would have happened would have been at the end of the case, because all the other witnesses would not have been lead and might not have been read, well, it simply would have been said we haven't proved our case. It is now apparent, and I needn't take you page by page to the support for this on a witness-by-witness basis, but it's now apparent that, in effect, for us to prove this case, we have to call basically all the witnesses. The Court may think, and in a sense I suspect both parties will be guided and assisted by the Court's reaction to both the dossier and the pleadings now filed in respect of it or the arguments filed in respect of it, the Court may think that where the Defence find themselves taking entirely technical arguments and providing no grounds for resistance beyond, for example, and I just open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice. Just to be clear, when you said you'll have to call all the witnesses, you mean the 170?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean as to Tulica, just looking at Tulica. I mean basically, from what they say, everything that every witness says is in dispute and I would have to call them all. Of course, I would be able to pare it down depending on which witnesses are available to me, and I would be able to make my own decision eventually as to when I was satisfied that I had got enough evidence in. But basically everything is going to have to be proved. There is not going to be the admission of any material fact. No underlying crime, and we heard this on the last occasion, is going to be conceded. In the words of Judge May on an earlier occasion, and reflecting the use of these terms in another jurisdiction, simply everything is going to be put in issue. It may be that the Chamber will think the Defence are on particularly weak ground in taking this approach, and I open it pretty much at random, page 35 of the Kordic response, where we see this, as part of their response to the statements of witnesses made: Paragraph 62: "The killing of Kasim Huseinovic was witnessed by Avdo and Akif Huseinovic. Avdo saw two or three soldiers striking Kasim Huseinovic with rifle butts and their boots. His skull seemed to have cracked open. His brain was visible. He was screaming and moaning, while the soldiers insisted that he give them his rifle. Kasim was then taken under escort to his house. When he came out of his house, the beating continued, and he was then shot and killed." Response: "Mr. Kordic has no knowledge of who, if anyone, was killed or by whom during military operations in the vicinity of Tulica in June of 1993. In addition, Mr. Kordic objects to any attempt to use either witness statements from witnesses who are not available to testify or testimony that they've given in other cases because there are no exceptional circumstances that might justify the admission of such testimony at this stage of the case under the holding of the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber decision." There it is. Let me be blunt. It is unlikely in the extreme that these witnesses are making up those allegations. To seek to block that evidence coming in in a short and convenient way is not helpful. It is aimed solely at taking advantage of being able to restrict noncontroversial material coming to the Chamber, and as I've said before, that's something that Defence are entirely entitled to do, and in some jurisdictions, perhaps many, it's a proper and justifiable approach from which they can be moved only by either the rules of court, and that is general rules, or by decisions made by a particular Trial Chamber, which is why we bring the matter to you. They don't have any grounds for challenging this material, and yet they say unless it's called live, you shouldn't have it. This is a problem not just for this case in this Tribunal but, of course, for other cases of this scale that will be coming to face this Tribunal, and it's a problem this Chamber may think that is best dealt with now.
