We would say, in relation to these responses, that it is quite insufficient, as a response, to resist the proper reading of the witness statements that support matters of that sort and that that material should be available to the Chamber in a convenient way, either in the form of the witness statements themselves, in the form of the report prepared by the investigator, or even, although it's now probably too brief a document, the document we served many months ago, the document that Mr. Stein said on the last occasion was the very sort of document that he would have pleaded to. You remember, he said there was a document he would have pleaded to if it had been in a particular form, and lo and behold, we had already served it in that form and they denied each and every word of that. That's the short form of summary about Tulica that was attached to the pre-trial brief and served earlier. So there is no ground for resisting this sort of material. In a trial of this kind where you're taking material from one part of the world and making it available for judges in another part of the world, it is frankly unrealistic to think that each and every piece of material has got to be here in person before it can be of value to the Tribunal. That's unrealistic. At the moment, I would rather not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, if I understand your position well, you're saying that there are documents taken from other cases in the same Tribunal regarding certain facts. Even if the accused has no knowledge of it, and the accused doesn't necessarily have to know everything that happened, does that mean that, in your view, the Defence may call those witnesses to cross-examine them, if they consider it necessary? You are satisfied with the documents produced in another case, and then the Defence, for its part, could they call the same witnesses to cross-examine them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I think that the documents we are concerned with primarily are witness statements that are taken not in other cases but taken by the Tribunal generally. They may have been taken specifically for this case and they may have been taken for another case, but they've been taken by investigators of the Tribunal. What we say is that they should be available to be read and that it shouldn't be required of us to call these witnesses to the Tribunal simply on the basis that Mr. Kordic has no knowledge of this sort of detail. We refer back to what we hoped was a correct reflection of the civil system as practised in some countries, and in particular in France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No. My question relates to any kind of documents. They may be statements or the transcript. But what about the right to cross-examine? That is the specific question, the right to cross-examine of the Defence. Supposing that, as far as you were concerned, you would produce statements which could be read. You do not necessarily have to have them reread, in a sense, in the Trial Chamber, but what about the right to cross-examine? What would you do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'll recall, Your Honour, the way we dealt with that on the previous occasion and the position we adopt today is that the right to cross-examine is not a right to cross-examine the observer or the hearer of any particular event. This material can be brought before the Chamber as evidence by the investigator in the way that we propose. The investigator can be cross-examined, he being the witness. He can be asked questions about the way in which statements are taken. He can be asked questions about what was known about the particular witnesses. He can be asked questions, if such questions can be founded, about any inconsistencies between statement and statement. On the basis of that cross-examination, the Chamber would be well positioned to decide whether the hearer or the observer should then be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, excuse me. I'm afraid we have to go down to the facts, sir. We've read all this, and with a great deal of interest. It's an interesting legal discussion and an important one. But the Defence says that this investigator is telling us hearsay evidence, it was not he who did the enquiries, they were collected by others, and, "We have the right to verify how those statements were collected." That is what the Defence is saying. What are you going to respond? Anyway, they are going to tell us themselves. Clearly, the fact that the accused has no knowledge is not an argument in itself, but the fact that it is hearsay and that they want to verify it themselves, what this investigator is saying, what are you going to respond to that? After all, this is a fundamental right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If your concern or if the concern is that the investigator didn't take any, bar one, of the particular witness statements, that of course can easily enough be remedied because we can call the other investigators who can therefore say what they can about the taking of the particular witness statements. As to whether the individual named in the witness statement, the person who saw or heard something, is to be cross-examined, I revert to our previous position that there is no enshrined right to that. That is a misunderstanding and a misreading of the Rules. The witness can produce the statement. The witness can be cross-examined. As I understand it from my time here, hearsay is an alien concept known only to one or two jurisdictions and is not a concept of general application in the civil system, applying different tests and in different ways, and if one sets aside and carves out from one's mind the prejudgements that may be there, because of years of working with hearsay, and one advances on the basis that material of any kind is capable of being evidence, thus the investigator in this case is capable of producing a witness statement, much as he is capable of producing a map or, in an appropriate case, the revolver or item of clothing, the Chamber is able, under its Rules, to consider the statement that he produces because it is capable of being evidence. The Chamber has to make its decision whether to consider that material. What we have suggested is that not only is the Chamber in a position to consider that material, but it can take a measure of control of proceedings by deciding not only that it can decide at some stage whether to attend to the witness statement's material, but it can actually decide whether that witness is one who ought to be called, thus doing, in large part, the job that the investigating judge does in some civil systems and thus getting over the roadblock that the Defence are putting in the way of this trial being conducted in a swift and compact way. What we've envisaged is that the investigator could be asked questions, if there are any that occur to the Defence as appropriate to ask him. I'm so sorry. The witness could be asked questions. We have no difficulty in calling the other investigators to answer particular questions about particular individuals. But if at the end of that exercise, and I come back, for example, to the page I picked pretty much at random, if at the end of that exercise, looking at paragraph 56, there was absolutely no reason to doubt the broad accuracy or, indeed, the detailed accuracy of what can be found at tab 16 and tab 10, or to take note of the next paragraph, which is perhaps similarly expressed, tab 16 and tab 10 again, or tab 9 at the foot of the page, if the Tribunal, having heard what the Defence raises, concludes that there is no good reason for doubting the broad accuracy of those people on those topics, then it could say to itself, "This is evidence. It's been produced to us in the form of a transcript or in the form of a statement. We see no reason to devalue it to nothing or, indeed, to devalue it at all, and we will attend to it." On my understanding, that is what happens in the civil systems. The judges, perhaps first the examining judge and then the trial judge, if he's sitting with a jury and perhaps with some other judges, makes the decision alone or collectively as to which witnesses should be called, bearing in mind the overarching interests of the due administration of justice, which has to reflect the time taken by due process, and the judge at the trial can have read out, for incorporation in the decision-making process, parts of written statements, and providing they are read out, they become evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is a United Kingdom Act, the Criminal Evidence or Criminal Justice Act, which deals with the situation of a person's statement being read into evidence when that statement has been collected abroad. The particular case that I have in mind, I'm sorry I don't have it here, because it wasn't clear to me that we were going to deal with it today. That particular case dealt with the argument as to whether what the Prosecution sought to do was consistent with the particular Article in the European Convention that guaranteed the right to examine and have examined, in the same circumstances as the Prosecution, witnesses. The English Act sets out a set of circumstances in which the statement can be admitted, and interestingly one of them is whether, in the absence of the right to cross-examine, because there would be no right to cross-examine, the statement would be read, whether in the absence of that right, there would be available to the Defence some means of testing the evidence, of objecting to it, some means of contradicting it. In that particular case, the Court concluded that the statement should not be read because the essential requirement of the Act, which was broadly based on admitting the evidence in the interests of justice, that requirement was not met. But I point to it because that's an Act coming from a country with which we are very familiar, and I was very attracted to the importance that the Act attached to the possibility of the Defence being able to contradict the statement in the absence of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in this case -- first of all, I must look that case up to see what guidance it can provide us, and I hope we can do that overnight. But in this case, if the Chamber were to decide that particular witnesses should be read because the Defence, in the American terminology, had not made a sufficient showing of cause why they should not be read, that would not, of course, restrict the Defence from calling evidence themselves to the contrary effect at a later stage, if it became available to them. The only thing that might trouble the Chamber in those circumstances would be if they hadn't revealed their knowledge of contradictory material, thus to sharpen the issue of whether the witness should be read at an earlier stage or not. So there's nothing to stop them contradicting it by other evidence, and the Chamber might think that the Defence, in this setting, has nothing to gain by hiding what material it would have to contradict these witnesses from the Chamber, and indeed, in raw terms, would be under a duty to let them know at this stage what material there is to contradict these witnesses. We see from their response that there is none. So I don't know if this is the answer to your question. I hope it is. A, they can contradict it, if there's material available, but, B, as things stand at the present, it would appear there is none and no reason to doubt these witnesses. Since you refer to the Great Britain, or the England and Wales jurisdiction, it is of course helpful for us all to remember that in that jurisdiction, there is now a presumption that written statements taken broadly in this way will become evidence in a case unless there is specific notice given that the witness needs to be called. Of course, in that jurisdiction, with which we are all a bit more familiar, although Defence can, if they wish, looking at a long list of 100 or 200 witnesses, demand their attendance, each and every one of them, they will be in for some very unpleasant surprises if they call witnesses wholly unnecessarily, continuity witnesses or witnesses whose evidence is noncontroversial. They may even find themselves subject to penal sanctions and costs in our English courts, for the development of the legal system in that country, and it may be elsewhere, is in line with our desire in this Tribunal, that avoidable expense and energy should not be wasted when things are not genuinely in issue. So I don't know if I answer your first question satisfactorily, but I hope I properly borrow the practice coming from that country for another purpose. Of course, there's a lot of complaint made by the Defence about these witness statements and whether they are taken by the investigators or, in certain other cases, taken in respect of people, I think, when they were leaving refugee camps and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A lot of complaint is made about these statements, and they picked on one or two particular points in the evidence so far. But the Chamber may reflect on the evidence you've heard so far, and I think in all material respects, witnesses have said what is contained in their statements, and it is fanciful to think that witnesses are going to be just making up wholly fictitious stories about attacks on the ground. That is not to say that where there is a specific and discreet issue about whether a village was defended, who were the soldiers attacking it and so on, or I suppose even whether it was an attack as opposed to a mere battle between equal sides or whatever is being contended, not to say that those may not be issues properly before the Chamber. That's a different issue. But that apart, witness statements have nearly always been matched by the evidence that is being given by the witnesses and the matters picked on by the Defence are either explicable, trivial, or outside that general proposition. The Chamber is left with this -- it's not a dilemma, in our respectful submission -- is left with this position, that if these defendants in this case are allowed to say, "We will admit nothing," I don't blame them for doing it or trying to do it, understand that, providing they don't couple it with protestations of co-operation or genuine desire to have the case over quickly, that that can't be their true state of mind. If the defendants in this case are allowed to say, in respect of matters of which they have no knowledge, the matter is in dispute notwithstanding a run of witness statements that go to establish it, why then that is followed in this Tribunal for other cases of this size, and the consequences are, I'm afraid to say, obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've got that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I understand, simply to make the point, that there are other cases -- for example, in your sister Tribunal -- where things are well capable of proceeding entirely otherwise and where huge masses of facts can be admitted, the case proceeds on the single issue, which might, indeed, be the single issue in this case. Given the underlying crimes, what's the connection of the defendant, which is what the issue is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Looking at the dossier for a moment, and breaking it down into its constituent parts, you've got the witness statements, first of all, which are heavily disputed. You've then got the transcripts of evidence of, I think, three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point made by the Defence in relation to them is that there are no exceptional circumstances which Aleksovski mentioned to admit those transcripts. What do you say in answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exceptional circumstances are the fact that these may be issues not shown to be truly in dispute; that there is therefore no need for the witnesses, in truth, to be bothered on such issues as the Chamber may decide this proposition is good. In those circumstances, just as with the statements themselves, it is material you can properly consider and read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next series of items which are disputed are the reports, contemporary reports, some of them, of forensic and other witnesses. What is objected to is that they should be subject to the usual procedures of the Trial Chamber, of the Tribunal, in relation to expert evidence. What do you say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are already pursuing a very broad policy on both sides in relation to documents and reports from monitors -- reports, indeed, from Mr. McLeod, although he came to speak to it himself -- all sorts of reports are being referred to. These reports, as contemporaneous documents, are documents likely to be accurate and reliable. There is no good ground shown for challenging their process or conclusions, and until there is, they should be admitted into evidence. If, on any particular or discrete issue, some controversial matter is identified, then we might respond differently. But at present it would be a nonsense -- if one goes to tab 19, where I think all sides are represented, insofar as it's possible to refer to sides -- it's a nonsense to think that somebody has got to come along and support each and every word of this report in the absence of good reason to the contrary. The report is a document that this Chamber can consider. And, if I may respectfully say so, isn't this the way that the Chamber's mind, collectively and individually, would work? If such documents are admitted, if in the course of cross-examination of the reporting investigator, Raatikainen, nothing is advanced to show why this document may be unreliable, and if at no other stage in the Prosecution case, to any witness to whom it could be raised, there is no question showing why this report may be unreliable, then the Court would probably be minded to accept it for full value, insofar as it would be helpful at the stage of judgement. If, in the course of the defence, something new emerged that could have been advanced earlier, the Chamber might be critical of the Defence for not having raised it earlier. If something emerged that could not reasonably have been raised earlier, it would not be critical of the Defence. But in either case, it might be minded to allow the matter to be dealt with, insofar as it could then be dealt with, in rebuttal. But absent the need for rebuttal evidence, the material which may well, in reality, be noncontroversial, would go in and would go in swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The death certificates: I find it hard to think that they are, in truth, controversial. Of course, there is always the potential for approaching us and negotiating any particular and identifiable problems about particular exhibits or documents; but otherwise, I really cannot see the Chamber's time should be taken with proving each and every one of these deaths. Likewise for all the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may be in a position tomorrow better to suggest -- supposing the Chamber were to come to the conclusion that there is no way that it can use this dossier in a positive way, and that it's simply got to be an old-fashioned, slog-it-out battle, then I may be in a better position tomorrow to identify the bare minimum of witnesses that I would forecast needing to call. But to some extent, I'm in a difficulty. One of the witnesses, an important witness, is at present not disposed to come, and he is an above-the-line witness, on our earlier formulation. It would be necessary, if he remains unwilling to come, and if it's necessary to do things by calling evidence on all topics, to substitute for him others who could cover the same ground. Can I, before I sit down, and not seeking to overload anyone with procedural alternatives that will confuse, nevertheless remind you of other ways of dealing with this problem, without recommending them particularly. One is, of course, that I think the Chamber can itself probably take evidence elsewhere. Two -- this is really in relation to unwilling witnesses -- two, it can take evidence by an appointed officer in the form of deposition or the equivalent. And although this may not be appropriate at this stage of this case -- or it may not be appropriate at any stage of any case, but it's worth thinking about -- witnesses in Bosnia can always be seen by the Defence investigator, but only on terms that they notify us when they are going to see those witnesses, Prosecution witnesses. Of course, such visits, if made, whether made on their own or on notice to us and in the presence of our investigators, could readily enough identify whether there is anything in issue at all. All saving the Tribunal's time -- well, saving the Chamber's time, although imposing work on others. Those are probably things to have in the backs of your minds rather than elsewhere, because there are limits to how many processes we can explore, given the reaction that we've received from the Defence in this case, which is at the stage it is. At this stage, we would invite to you say that the Chamber now knows, from the Defence, what are the real issues; from that, it will be able to identify the issues upon which evidence should be led, leaving it to the Defence to establish what other issues, if they're not happy with the Chamber's ruling, should be the subject of evidence here, and the Chamber should be prepared to read the balance of the material, or, alternatively, to read it in the summarised form of the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith. You've got about ten minutes now, and we'll hear you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is really, in our judgement, and I think I must say it at the outset, quite appalling to hear the argument made by the Prosecutor. The right of confrontation, in order to determine whether material presented is true, is accurate, in order to test the credibility of witnesses, in order to test their powers of observation, in order to determine whether there is matter to be challenged, is the heart of the rights assured to a defendant in a criminal proceeding, both in the civil law and in the common law, and in the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, which is being applied both to civil law and common-law systems. Our papers reflect these rights, and the way in which they have developed, over hundreds of years. They reflect the trend in the European Court of Human Rights law -- and I will discuss that at some length tomorrow -- particularly because the language employed in that convention is exactly, or virtually exactly, the same language as is employed in the international covenant that was referred to by Judge Robinson earlier and is the same language, exactly the same language, that appears in the Statute of this Tribunal as a guarantee of minimum rights of due process to defendants appearing before this Tribunal. The case law of the European Court of Human Rights involves cases against organised crime, cases against terrorists, cases that have equal societal significance in terms of the rights of the State and the rights of the public. And those cases uniformly would reject, as I will explain in greater detail tomorrow, the use of this dossier, of the witness statements, in evidence, without witnesses, and the use of reports of investigators, even where investigators are available to be cross-examined. And you are not hearing about that case law from the Prosecutor, and you're not hearing about the evolution in the civil law and the requirement that an investigating judge take matters in sworn testimony, subject to the laws of perjury. The suggestion, for example, that the ability, if it did exist, and I suspect the persons would not agree, but suppose witnesses for the Prosecution were to agree to be interviewed by the Defence, those statements to the Defence, which the Prosecution would have us use as our right of confrontation to develop whether there is an issue, would not be sworn, they would not be subject to the laws of perjury, and quite to the contrary, from what my learned colleague has said, there has been material divergence. Not once, not twice, but over and over again. The genius of the criminal law is understanding that something is not God-given truth just because it is said to be the case. That is what the whole right of confrontation is about. That is what we have spent hundreds of years developing the right of confrontation for. Defendants are not obligated to provide cause, specific to each fact or each document or each witness, before they get the right of confrontation. The right of confrontation is the vehicle by which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if you're right about this. Of course, historically, the right of confrontation is a most important right for an accused person in a criminal trial. We understand that. So therefore, if there's a matter which is particularly in issue, if your client is mentioned in a particular way, then it's most important that the evidence is given properly and he has the right to cross-examine about it. But if there are other matters about which there so far seems to have been little controversy and little cross-examination -- for instance, that there were a number of people killed at a particular location -- should the Defence have the right to insist upon the presence of witnesses just to see whether there is some point that they can raise, when so far there has been very little controversy about it? Besides the interest which you mentioned, there is the public interest in an expeditious and fair -- and that means fair to both sides -- trial. And that's got to be put in the balance, hasn't it? Therefore, why is it unreasonable to require the Defence to indicate what prejudice is caused in these circumstances by witnesses to these matters having material put before the Tribunal in different ways? What is the unfairness to your client in the particular case? That is the issue that I would find it helpful for you to address. Of course, I understand the point, the general point, the general principle. But it is the facts of the case that have got to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Let me do that briefly, Your Honour, now, and we will address that in greater detail in the morning -- or in the afternoon, since we have afternoon sessions both this week and next. The first thing to understand, and the grounding point in the Defence argument, is that the alleged attacks, whether as to killing of persons, wounding of persons, destruction of property, plunder of property, in each of the villages alleged in the indictment, and of which Tulica is one example, are elements of the offence that must be proved by the Prosecutor in addition to his proof that the defendant is linked, either because he directly participated in the attacks, or he is linked because of other facts and circumstances which lead to vicarious liability, either under an aiding-and-abetting theory under 7(1) or command responsibility under 7(3). So from the Defence point of view, every single attack alleged as a war crime is fundamentally important, because if it is not proved, the defendant cannot be guilty, even if he were there in person, much less if there were vicarious linkage. So that's the first point, and Tulica is alleged, counts 7 to 13 and 30 to 39, injury and property damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But when you say "proved," do you mean proved by having a witness standing up and proving every element, a series of witnesses? Is that what you envisage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If there is a necessary element of a crime, the Prosecutor has the burden of going forward, the Prosecutor has the burden of proof, and there is a presumption of innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. But you are saying, so that I understand the position, that all has to be proved by oral evidence: Every document's got to be proved by a witness, or the witness comes here and gives evidence directly. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There are obviously rules about hearsay; there are obviously rules, as Your Honours have interpreted them, about foundations for documents. But the wholesale use of witness statements without witnesses, or prior testimony without exceptional circumstances, as proposed by the Prosecution, or investigators' reports of what witnesses said, is a completely different matter than the normal accommodations incident to any criminal proceeding, in terms of whether every single piece of evidence must come from the mouth of an individual. My colleague, Mr. Stein, will address this in greater length tomorrow. I hope I have come close to answering Your Honour's question, and I perhaps ought to close today by simply saying that the European Court of Human Rights has faced these issues over and over and has a developed case law on the question of, quote, examined and have examined, close quote, and it has faced the question of the countervailing public rights and needs in the context of organised crime, in the context of terrorists, and it has recognised that expediency cannot override the fundamental rights of the defendant. They have struggled in the case law, they have struggled with this issue manfully; and the case law, in our judgement, is clearly decisive that this wholesale use would not be permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the other issue is the scale and the scope of cases of this sort. Of course, the case law is important, but none of them, none of those cases deal with an international crime of this particular dimension and magnitude, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think Your Honour may be correct, although cases involving organised crime are frequently very complex and involve a great many facts and witnesses, depending on the case. But I will plan to start my argument on the merits dealing with the question whether there really is a problem at this stage in the case, and whether we haven't already gotten to the point, by grinding down the rough edges with the tools already available to the Chamber, where this case can be tried efficiently without trampling on the rights of any of the parties. Shall we commence in the morning, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow. Mr. Nice, you've got one witness who will be short; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, he will be very short, as far as I'm concerned. He is the witness who took the statement from Dr. Mujezinovic that lies at the root of all sorts of complaints by the Defence, and therefore he had better be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear him at half past 2.00 and then go on with the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of July, 1999, at 2.30 p.m.
